Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Students sort cards on their phones without being told they’re values. Don’t say “values” until the reveal slide.

Every student in the room

Family, faith, culture and community count as values just as much as independence or adventure; say so at the reveal, and never ask anyone which value they starred.

Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

Keep it light for ten seconds, then go straight to the next slide.

Slide 2 · Notes

No names needed. Take a few call-outs and write the words on the board: shows up, honest, funny, loyal, calm. Don’t call them values yet. Leave the board up for the reveal.

Slide 3 · Notes

Six minutes. Share the link (QR, Canvas, or the chat). Students without a device circle five on the Who’s Driving? values card and star one. Early finishers can screenshot their card.

Slide 4 · Notes

Point to the warm-up words on the board: “Same kind of words. You picked the people in your corner for their values, and now you’ve picked yours.” Family, faith, culture and community count as much as freedom or adventure.

Slide 5 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 6 · Notes

Cohen et al. (Science, 2006): 7th graders who wrote about their top value did a bit better, most for Black students facing stereotype threat. Larger trials found less (Borman 2016; Hanselman 2017), so don’t oversell it. Bryan, Yeager et al. (2016): teens changed what they did when a choice was about their own independence and fairness.

Slide 7 · Notes

One minute each. Nobody has to reveal their star.

Slide 8 · Notes

Take a few. Then three quick moments, one at a time.

Slide 9 · Notes

Pick any value and say what it would do, in one line you’d actually say. Hear a few.

Slide 10 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 11 · Notes

Same move. Point out that family is a value at the wheel.

Slide 12 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 13 · Notes

Hear a few lines. Two different values can lead to the same good move.

Slide 14 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 15 · Notes

Quiet. The writing box is at the bottom of their results card and is never saved. Students who’d rather not write can just think.

Slide 16 · Notes

If a student’s values pull against home, say both can be true: you can honor your family and still notice what matters to you.

Slide 17 · Notes

Close with: “Nobody can tell you what your values are, and no quiz can either. You just noticed them. Use them.” If anything heavy came up, thank the student and let a counselor know that day.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students sort 32 cards on instinct, keep five, star one, and only then learn that what they sorted are their values. They see one way their star value could steer a real moment, and write privately about why it matters. Nobody shares their list.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • A phone or laptop per student, or one per pair (students without one can circle five on the Who’s Driving? values card)
  • A board for the warm-up words
  • The Gut Check link to share (click the phone slide to open it)

Flow

  1. 2 minWarm-up: someone you’d want in your corner
  2. 6 minThe Gut Check, quietly on phones
  3. 3 minThe reveal, and what the research says
  4. 5 minTurn and talk, share out, then three moments
  5. 2 minTwo minutes, just for you
  6. 2 minEvery student, close

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

Warm-up, the Gut Check, the reveal, and one moment. Students write on their own later.

Before you teach
Keep the reveal.

The point is that students pick on instinct before the word "values" shows up and they start choosing what sounds good. If someone asks, say "you'll see at the end."

Nobody shares their list.

Turn-and-talk is about what a value would do in a moment, not which one you starred. Students can talk about any value, theirs or not.

When values pull against home.

A student whose star is independence may live in a family that prizes making them proud, or the other way around. Both can be true at once. If it seems to weigh on someone, mention that counselors are good to talk to about exactly that.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Values come from many places.

For some students, values come from their family, faith or community more than from themselves. The cards include family, faith, culture and heritage, making my family proud, and community on purpose. Treat those as their own choices, not someone else driving.

Faith, and no faith.

Faith is one card among 32. Students who aren't religious skip it; students who are can star it. Neither needs explaining.

Devices and reading.

Students can work in pairs on one phone, use the paper card, or have the cards read aloud. The page works with a screen reader and keyboard.

What the research says

The Personal Values Card Sort, used in motivational interviewing, has people sort value cards into piles by how important each is, then rank the top ones. It is in the public domain.

Miller, C'de Baca, Matthews & Wilbourne, University of New Mexico, 2001

Seventh graders who wrote for a few minutes about their most important value early in the year earned somewhat better grades, with the largest effect for Black students facing stereotype threat.

Cohen, Garcia, Apfel & Master, Science, 2006

In a larger trial across many schools, the effect was smaller, and a large replication found little overall effect.

Borman et al., 2016; Hanselman et al., Journal of Educational Psychology, 2017

Teens changed their choices for months when a choice was framed around their own values, like independence and fairness, rather than adult rules.

Bryan, Yeager et al., PNAS, 2016
